title: Multi-AZ
subtitle: Intra-region fault domains, synchronous consensus across 3 AZs, and cross-AZ network costs.
keyTakeaways: An Availability Zone (AZ) consists of one or more physically isolated data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking, linked by low-latency (<2ms) dark fiber.
Production stateful quorums (Raft, Paxos, Zookeeper) require at least 3 AZs: a 2-AZ setup cannot safely form a majority quorum if either AZ disconnects, risking split-brain or total stall.
Cross-AZ traffic is billed by major cloud providers in both directions; high-throughput clusters use Topology-Aware Routing to keep RPC calls and cache lookups within the local zone.

sections.heading: Physical Isolation and the Three-AZ Quorum Rule
sections.body: A single data center can be knocked offline by transformer failures, cooling pipeline bursts, or local fiber cuts. Cloud regions group three or more physically isolated Availability Zones within a metropolitan area, connected by high-bandwidth, redundant dark fiber.
bullets: Sub-2ms synchronous boundary: Round-trip network latency between AZs inside the same region is typically between 0.5ms and 2ms. This low latency makes synchronous database replication and Raft/Paxos consensus practical without degrading API performance.

Why two AZs are insufficient for consensus: A majority quorum requires floor(N/2) + 1 votes. In a 2-AZ cluster with 2 nodes (one in each AZ), losing one AZ leaves the surviving node with only 1 out of 2 votes (50%), which is not a majority. It cannot safely elect a leader or accept writes without risking split-brain.

Three-AZ quorum resilience: Distributing 3 consensus nodes across 3 distinct AZs ensures that if any single AZ goes dark, the remaining 2 nodes still hold a 2/3 majority (66%), electing a leader and maintaining write availability automatically.

codeSnippet.title: Kubernetes Topology Spread Constraints & Zone-Aware Routing
codeSnippet.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payment-service
spec:
  replicas: 6
  template:
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: payment-service
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payment-service
  annotations:
    # Prefer routing traffic to pods within the caller's same AZ
    service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto

sections.heading: Cross-AZ Data Transfer Costs and Zonal Affinity
sections.body: While spreading microservices across 3 AZs provides fault tolerance, naive round-robin load balancing results in roughly 66% of all internal RPC traffic crossing AZ boundaries, generating substantial cloud network bills.
bullets: The cross-AZ billing tax: Cloud providers charge for network traffic crossing AZ boundaries ($0.01 to $0.02 per GB in each direction). In a high-throughput microservice architecture passing terabytes of data daily across deep call graphs, cross-AZ transfer fees can rival compute costs.

Topology-Aware Routing: Configure Kubernetes and service proxies (such as Envoy) to route traffic to pod replicas residing in the same AZ whenever healthy pods are available locally, crossing the AZ boundary only as a failover fallback.

Topology spread constraints: Use Kubernetes `topologySpreadConstraints` with `maxSkew: 1` across `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` to guarantee that application pods are distributed evenly across all three zones, preventing any single AZ failure from taking down more than a third of capacity.

tradeOffs.pros: Distributes compute and memory utilization evenly across all instances regardless of uneven ingress traffic per zone.
tradeOffs.cons: Incurs cross-AZ transfer fees on 66% of calls and adds 1 to 2ms of network latency per microservice hop.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Low-throughput, CPU-bound services where compute utilization balance is more important than network transfer costs.

tradeOffs.pros: Eliminates cross-AZ network egress charges and shaves 1 to 2ms of latency off each RPC hop.
tradeOffs.cons: Can cause uneven CPU load or hot-spotting if one AZ receives disproportionately high external ingress traffic.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput Kafka streaming, distributed in-memory caches, and chatty multi-tier microservice architectures.

interviewTip: Always explain why stateful consensus clusters require 3 AZs rather than 2: in a 2-AZ setup, losing either AZ drops the cluster to 50% voting capacity, making it impossible to form a safe majority quorum without risking split-brain.
